Epicurus. Born in three hundred and forty-one BCE, died in two hundred and seventy BCE. He was a Greek philosopher who founded an influential school teaching that pleasure is the highest good. But there's a twist. By "pleasure" he didn't mean hedonistic excess. He meant the absence of pain and fear. His ethical system was grounded in atomism and a radically naturalistic worldview, and it has been systematically misrepresented since antiquity.

Epicurus was born on the island of Samos and spent most of his life in Athens. He founded the Garden, a philosophical community emphasizing simple living, friendship, and intellectual discussion. Unlike Plato's Academy, the Garden welcomed women and slaves as students—something extraordinary for the time. He wrote over three hundred works, but most are lost. What we know comes mainly from letters preserved by Diogenes Laërtius.

His ethics redefined hedonism entirely. Pleasure, he taught, is not indulgence but the absence of pain, which he called aponia, and mental disturbance, which he called ataraxia. He advocated modest living. Bread, water, and simple vegetables—that was his recommendation. Luxury and excess, he argued, create dependency and anxiety. Friendship is the highest good because it combines mutual benefit, loyalty, and freedom from fear. He drew a crucial distinction between necessary desires—food, shelter, basic security—and vain desires like wealth, fame, and luxury.

For his physics, Epicurus adopted atomism. The universe is atoms and void, governed by mechanical causation. Atoms are eternal, indivisible, and infinite. Motion and collision are eternal. But he added something unique: atoms swerve randomly, a small deviation he called the clinamen. This random swerve allows for human free will and moral responsibility. Matter, he insisted, is not divine. The gods exist, he said, but they take no interest in human affairs. This removes divine judgment as a source of fear.

His reputation has suffered terribly. In antiquity he was called Epicurean as a slur meaning hedonist. Christians and Stoics attacked him relentlessly. Medieval and Renaissance thinkers equated Epicureanism with gluttony—a grossly unfair stereotype. Modern scholarship recognizes him as an ascetic philosopher whose ethics advocate modest pleasure grounded in physical and mental tranquility. His insistence that women and slaves belong in a philosophical community was radical for his time.
